title: Cutting It Out
logline: A chena farmer finally decides to dig out, root and all, a weed that has come back every season for years, choosing the harder work now over the easier work every year after.
human_question: What is the real difference between managing a problem and ending it?

premise.story: A farmer working a slash-and-burn plot faces a deep-rooted, recurring weed and chooses between the usual seasonal cutting-back and the much harder work of digging it out completely.
premise.place: A chena (shifting cultivation) plot in the dry zone.
premise.experience: Physical, unglamorous labour that stands in for a real and recognisable choice: quick relief now, or harder work that actually finishes the problem.

concept_links.why: The source's own image for a path mind's permanent effect is exactly this: holding a harmful tendency down for a while versus cutting it off at the root so it cannot come back, like felling a young tree before it fruits [C016-P:L76–L82].
The balance the farmer needs, patient digging without giving up, but not so much force that the tool breaks, echoes the source's repeated theme of balanced, sustained effort [C076-P:L783].

what_camera_could_observe: The familiar weed found again this season, the farmer's decision
The harder digging work: roots traced and pulled, not just cut
The cleared ground, and what is planted or left in its place
The following season, if filming allows, showing whether it returns
what_must_be_real: A real farmer's real land and real choice. The film should not suggest the digging succeeds if, in fact, the weed returns.

possible_arc.opening: The weed found again, as every year.
possible_arc.turn: The decision to dig, not cut.
possible_arc.ending_open: The cleared ground, and, if time allows, the next season's check.

requirements: A working chena farmer with a real recurring weed problem
A filming schedule that can follow at least one full clearing
Ideally, a return visit the following season

suggestions.name: A chena farming area
suggestions.why: Slash-and-burn cultivation is still practised in parts of the dry zone.
suggestions.verify: A specific willing farmer must be identified.

risks: Treating a farmer's practical choice as a moral lesson
Chena cultivation can be a sensitive land-use topic; avoid taking a position on it
Overstating what one cleared season proves
drop_if: No farmer will let a real land decision be filmed, or the metaphor would misrepresent their actual reasoning, which is driven by labour and cost, not by any wider point

connections.note: Both ask whether a change is temporary or complete, one through a crossing, one through a farmer's choice about a weed.
The same question asked through a person's habit rather than a field.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed. Everything above is a research direction.
